enrichment_summary: Revised: the claim below about the schematic PDF having no extractable text only applies to that PDF file itself — this core's documentation separately holds 18 pre-cropped schematic page images (per-page, human-legible scans, not the same asset as Schematics.pdf), all of which have now been reviewed directly. That review found many real, previously-undocumented facts — see schematic_findings below for the full write-up (board sub-designations, CPU/oscillator/reset detail, a factory test/ICE header on the CPU bus, program-ROM bus decoding, sprite and background pixel shift-register organization, sprite Y-range compare logic, PAL-based priority/color-select logic, dipswitch/IO decoding, controls/coin conditioning, the PSG/audio-amp circuit, RGB DAC detail, and the full inter-board interconnect including a previously-undocumented NMI line). The supplied 'Hardware Reference' material is the generic MAME netlist engine changelog (audio/nl_konami.cpp, solver internals, etc.) and does not reference Technos, the TA-0010 board, or any AY8910/discrete-logic circuitry used by this game — mystston's audio path is driven directly by two AY8910 PSGs via MAME's ay8910 device, not the netlist analog solver, so none of that changelog is applicable here.

schematic_findings.source: Cropped schematic pages (distinct from the textless Schematics.pdf) — drawing number K-10848, sheet series 'MPX-01', dated 60.6.4 (Showa 60 = 1985-06-04), drafted by データイースト株式会社 (Data East Co., Ltd. — the schematic's drafting/production company per its title-block stamp; this is a document-production credit, not a claim about who published the game, which MAME/arcade-history already establish as Technos Japan).
schematic_findings.board_designations: Confirms board_spec.board.board_type's '2-PCB set' directly. TA-0010-P1 ('btm bd') carries: the CPU, reset circuit, master oscillator, hsync/vsync generation, the raw-CPU-bus test header, the program ROM bank and its bus-control decoding, sprite RAM/pattern address muxing, sprite tile ROMs and pixel shift registers, sprite Y-range compare logic, and the sprite line-buffer RAM plus priority/color-select PALs. TA-0010-P2 ('top bd') carries: the dipswitch/IO decoder, player-control and coin connectors, the two PSGs plus audio power amp, the RGB DAC/video output stage, and the background tilemap address muxing plus tile ROMs and pixel shift registers.
schematic_findings.cpu: The 40-pin DIP CPU is silkscreened/labeled '6502A' on the CPU-board schematic — the higher-speed-rated (2MHz) variant of the part, not a plain unmarked 6502 or a different manufacturer's second-source. Confirms board_spec.cpus[0].type="M6502" at the specific-part-number level.
schematic_findings.master_oscillator: The same CPU-board page shows crystal X1 = 12MHz directly, with a 470ohm/470ohm (R1/R2) + 0.1uF (C4) inverter-gate oscillator circuit, and a separately buffered '/2M' output alongside it. Confirms board_spec.clocks.master_hz=12000000 directly from the schematic (previously only sourced from the MAME driver's clock config, not the board documentation).
schematic_findings.reset_circuit: The CPU-board page also shows the CPU reset generator: an NE555 timer IC (power-on delay monostable) plus a manual reset pushbutton (SW1), feeding the 6502A's reset pin — not previously documented anywhere in board_spec.json. Not modeled as a discrete circuit in the FPGA core (jtframe's own reset/rst generation is used instead, which is the normal jtframe convention for this), but useful context for anyone comparing real power-on behavior against the core.
schematic_findings.cpu_bus_test_connector: A separate small header (distinct from the two main inter-board connectors) on the CPU board breaks out the raw 6502 bus under 'C'-prefixed net names: a full 16-bit CAD0-CAD15 address bus, an 8-bit CDB0-CDB7 data bus, plus C-R/W, C-phi2 (the CPU's phase-2 clock), CE and C0IN. This is almost certainly a factory test or in-circuit-emulator (ICE) connector for burning/testing ROMs or bench debugging during development — it plays no role in normal game operation and has no FPGA-core equivalent.
schematic_findings.program_rom_bus: The program-ROM bank (six 2764 EPROMs, 8KB each = 48KB total, matching board_spec.roms' maincpu region) is decoded through 74LS257-class address multiplexers and a small PROM/decoder stage producing distinctly-named chip-select nets — among them *BACK, *VRAM, *ZERO/ZERO, and *I/O — i.e. background RAM, video RAM, zero-page RAM, and I/O each get their own dedicated select line on real hardware, confirming the conventional 6502 memory-map split already reflected in board_spec.memory_map, now cross-checked against schematic net names rather than only MAME driver source.
schematic_findings.sprite_pixel_generation: Sprite graphics use the same generic technique as most mid-80s arcade hardware: three pairs of 2764 tile ROMs feed 74LS273-class latches and 74LS257-class muxes, which load into six 74LS194 (4-bit universal shift register) packages that serialize the pixel data out in sync with the pixel clock. A separate address-mux stage (built from 74LS257/74S225-class multiplexers) merges the CPU's address bus with the video-scan address so the same sprite RAM can be written by the CPU and read by the raster scanner — conceptually the same shared-bus arbitration mystston_obj.v performs internally, just implemented with real multiplexer ICs instead of an FPGA dual-port RAM.
schematic_findings.sprite_y_compare: A bank of XOR gates (74LS86-class) compares the sprite's stored Y position against the current raster line to produce OBJON/OBJLIN — the real-hardware equivalent of mystston_obj.v's own magnitude-compare check (is the current line within 16 of this sprite's Y). Same function, different technique: bit-position XOR-compare in hardware vs. an arithmetic compare in the FPGA core.
schematic_findings.sprite_linebuf_and_priority: The sprite line-buffer is built from two 2148-class (1Kx4) static RAMs, combined to store one 8-bit-wide scanline buffer of sprite pixel data — the real-hardware analogue of the FPGA core's own per-line sprite buffer arrays. Feeding into and alongside this buffer are two PAL16R4 chips and a PAL10L8, driving a 74LS374-class output latch labeled 'OBJCG' (object color generator). This is very likely where sprite/background layer priority and final color selection are actually decided on real hardware — see board_spec.video.layer_priority_logic for what this means for documentation confidence (the PAL equations themselves aren't recoverable without a fuse-map dump).
schematic_findings.background_pixel_generation: Background graphics use the identical technique to the sprite path, on the other board: three pairs of 2764 tile ROMs feed six 74LS194 shift registers to serialize background pixel data, with its own separate 74LS257/74S225-class address mux (built from XOR-gate logic combining the horizontal/vertical raster counters with the CPU address bus) generating the shared-bus background RAM address.
schematic_findings.dipswitches_io_decoder: The dipswitch/IO-decoder page (video-output board) shows two 8-position DIP switch banks with SIP pull-up resistor packs, buffered through 74LS244-class octal buffers, and latched through a 74LS273-class chip that produces several of the same chip-select-shaped net names seen elsewhere (dipswitch read strobes, a color-select line, an IRQ-clear line, and the AY8910 select/data-latch strobes referenced in board_spec.audio's BC1/BDIR notes) — i.e. the real dipswitch and AY8910-latch decoding share the same small decoder stage on this board.
schematic_findings.controls_coin_inputs: The controls/coin schematic page (video-output board) shows a full connector pinout for both players' 4-way joystick + 2 buttons + start, each line diode+RC filtered ahead of 74LS244-class buffering. Coin inputs are conditioned through 2SC1075 transistors (a real, legible part number) plus resistors, combining into one debounced 'COIN' line, with two separate NE555-based monostable circuits providing per-slot coin-pulse timing — a hardware debounce/pulse-shaping stage with no direct FPGA-core equivalent needed, since coin inputs there are typically just synchronized and edge-detected digitally.
schematic_findings.sound_psg_amp: The two AY-3-8910-equivalents are labeled directly 'PSG1'/'PSG2' on the sound schematic page (video-output board). Their outputs are mixed through a discrete resistor network (1K x3 per PSG bank into a shared 5.1K x6 bank covering all 6 AY channels, then a final 1K resistor) ahead of a 10K volume potentiometer and a Mitsubishi M51516 audio power-amp IC (a real, legible part number) that drives the cabinet speaker. The external audio connector also carries -5V and +12V supply pins alongside the amplified Sound+/Sound- output lines. A pair of 74LS273-class data/control latches feed the two PSGs, confirming the real hardware also uses a two-latch (data + control) scheme structurally similar to mystston_sound.v's own BC1/BDIR edge-detect emulation.
schematic_findings.video_timing_generation: The hsync-generator and vsync-generator schematic pages (both on the CPU board) build HSYNC/VSYNC/HBLK/VBLK entirely from small-scale binary counters and logic gates (74LS161/74LS157-class packages, by pin count and package outline) — no single custom video-timing chip is visible on either page, or anywhere else across the full 18-page schematic set now that all pages have been reviewed. This weakens (though can't with absolute certainty disprove a misread label) board_spec.video.custom_chips' 'HMC20' entry — see that field's own updated wording.
schematic_findings.rgb_dac: The video-output board's schematic confirms the RGB DAC circuit directly: three 2SC1815 NPN transistors (R/G/B channels) plus a fourth for a composite SYNC line, each driven through the resistor network already noted in board_spec.video.palette.notes (values on this page: R54=1.5K, R53=3.3K, R52=1.5K, R50=3.3K, R51=4.7K, R48=1.5K, R49=3.3K, R41=4.7K, labeled as 'resistor (color drive) values' — matches the previously-documented 4.7k/3.3k/1.5k taps exactly). Output connector J3 pins are individually labeled: B13=Blue, A13=Green, A14=Red, B14=Sync. CMPSYNC/CMPBLK (composite sync/blank, generated on the sync pages) feed this stage — the real board outputs composite sync to the monitor harness, not separate H/V sync lines; not something the FPGA core needs to reproduce (jtframe's own HS/VS/video pipeline already handles output framing its own, standard way), just a fact about the original hardware's connector.
schematic_findings.board_interconnect: The two PCBs are joined by two 40-of-50-pin flat cables (both explicitly annotated 'pins 41-50 left open'), carrying: the full shared address/data bus, R/W, E clock, reset, and *I/O and *BACK chip-select strobes on one cable; and the raster position counters (HLOC/VLOC), several video/color strobes (including the background- and sprite-color-generator outputs), composite sync/blank, and clock taps (12MHz-derived M4H, 6MHz, 1.5MHz) on the other. Both cables also carry a signal labeled *NMI crossing between the two boards — a real, physical non-maskable-interrupt line. Cross-checked against the FPGA core's own mystston_main.v: this matches its coin-insert NMI (`nmi = ~coin[0] | ~coin[1]`, mirroring mystston.cpp's coin_inserted()) exactly, confirming the real coin path is a hardware NMI rather than a polled input.

distribution.source: 12MHz master XTAL (X1, confirmed on the CPU-board schematic)
distribution.target: maincpu (6502A, confirmed on the same schematic page)
distribution.path: divide-by-8 (direct hardwired divider, per MAME driver clock config)
divide-by-8, shares the same derived 1.5MHz line as maincpu
divide-by-8, shares the same derived 1.5MHz line as maincpu and ay1
divide-by-2 to 6MHz pixel clock driving the 384x272 raster

video_enriched.dac_type: Resistor ladder (weighted-resistor network) driven by 2SC1815 NPN transistors, confirmed directly on the video-output board's schematic — not a dedicated DAC IC, matching pcb.notes' claim of no custom video silicon beyond the PAL/PROM parts
video_enriched.sync_generation: The hsync-generator and vsync-generator schematic pages (both on the CPU board) build HSYNC/VSYNC/HBLK/VBLK from small-scale discrete 74LS-class counters and gates — no part matching 'HMC20' (or any other single custom video-timing IC) is visible on either page, or anywhere else now that the full 18-page schematic set has been reviewed. See board_spec's video.custom_chips for the current confidence level.
video_enriched.layer_priority_logic: Resolved as far as documentation can go: the sprite line-buffer/color schematic page shows two PAL16R4 chips and a PAL10L8 feeding a 74LS374-class latch labeled 'OBJCG' (object color generator) — priority/color-select logic for the sprite and background layers appears to live inside these programmable parts. Their fuse equations aren't extractable from a schematic drawing (no JEDEC dump available), so the exact behavior can't be reverse-engineered from documentation alone. The FPGA core's own priority order (foreground > sprites > background, in mystston_colmix.v) was derived from MAME driver source and confirmed against hardware-monitor testing, independently of this finding.

additional_notes: All 18 schematic pages have now been reviewed. Beyond the RGB DAC/palette detail already cross-referenced into video_enriched.dac_type (2SC1815 driver transistors, R41/R48-R54 resistor values, J3 connector pinout), the fullest new material is: the PSG mixing network and M51516 audio-amp part number (previously an open gap — board_spec's audio.mixing described the emulated summing but not the real hardware), the sprite/background pixel-generation techniques (ROM-fed shift registers, address-mux sharing between CPU and raster scan), the PAL-based sprite priority/color-select logic (resolving the previously-unchecked layer_priority_logic question, at least as far as 'where it lives' if not the exact equations), and the inter-board interconnect detail including a previously-undocumented NMI line and a separate CPU-bus test/ICE header. See schematic_findings above for the complete write-up of each.
